Theos
thay-OSS
n. (Greek)
Greek theos, “God,” the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew Elohim (God) and occasionally for El; the chief noun for the deity throughout both testaments’ Greek text.

📖 Biblical Definition

Theos is the New Testament’s chief noun for God—the word used in the LXX to translate the Hebrew Elohim (the most common Hebrew word for God) and occasionally El, and used throughout the New Testament as the standard designation for the deity. The word is so structural that the New Testament’s opening verses can scarcely move without it: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God (theos), and the Word was God (theos) (John 1:1)—a verse that has structured Christian Trinitarian thought from the second century onward and that contains within it the deepest claim the apostles make about the deity of Christ. Two of the verse’s three uses of theos are articular (with the definite article ho theos) and one is anarthrous (without the article, simply theos); both grammatically distinct uses claim full deity, the second clause naming the Word as the same theos with whom He was eternally. The New Testament uses theos in several major theological contexts. Of the Father: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (John 3:16); blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Cor 1:3). Of the Son: and the Word was God (John 1:1); Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God (John 20:28); that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life (1 John 5:20); but unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever (Heb 1:8 quoting Ps 45:6); looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Tit 2:13); through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet 1:1). Of the Holy Spirit: the deity of the Spirit is implied by His person and work, though the explicit titular application of theos to the Spirit is rarer than to the Father and Son; Acts 5:3-4 sets the inference: Peter says Ananias has lied to the Holy Ghost and immediately to theos, making the equation. The doctrine of God in the New Testament is therefore structured around theos in its full applications: one God (Deut 6:4; 1 Cor 8:6; Eph 4:6), eternally existing in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—each of whom is properly named theos, sharing the one divine essence, distinguishable by their personal properties and relations. The Trinitarian doctrine the church confesses across the creeds is built upon the New Testament’s precise applications of theos to the three persons in their unity and distinction. Apart from the doctrine of God, every other doctrine collapses; with the doctrine of God set out from the New Testament’s use of theos, the whole Christian theology stands.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Theos: God; the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew Elohim; the chief noun designating the deity throughout the NT; applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit in their unity and distinction as the One God in three persons.

GOD, n. — The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite Spirit, the Creator, and the Sovereign of the universe. In scripture, applied principally to the True God, but also occasionally to false gods (with qualification), to angels, and to magistrates as representatives of divine authority.

THEOS — (Greek noun, G2316.) God; the chief NT noun for the deity. Over 1300 NT uses. Applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit; the foundation of Trinitarian doctrine.

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 20:28 — "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God."

Titus 2:13 — "Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ."

1 John 5:20 — "And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Theos is corrupted, in the contemporary religious landscape, by the generic-deism that treats God as a neutral category occupied differently by different religions—and by the heretical anti-Trinitarian movements (Arianism in its many recurrences, modalism in its modern forms, Jehovah’s Witness denial of Christ’s deity, Unitarianism) that refuse the New Testament’s precise application of theos to the Son and (by inference) the Holy Spirit alongside the Father.

expand to see more

Generic-deism is the contemporary cultural corruption of theos. The category God is treated as a neutral, common, religiously-pluralistic noun occupied differently by Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism (in its monotheistic strands), and the deism of philosophical theists. The implication—that the various religions are all reaching for the same God under different conceptions—is not what Scripture means by theos. The God of the Bible is the specific Trinity: one in essence, three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. To worship the God of the Bible is to worship the Trinity; to refuse the Trinity (as Islam, Judaism since the rejection of Christ, Unitarianism, and the various Christian heresies do) is to worship a different deity, however much the vocabulary overlaps. The recovery is the precise Trinitarian doctrine. The God Christians worship is not God in the generic sense but the Father, the Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, one God in three persons; the gospel announces the Father’s love for the world expressed in the Son’s incarnation, cross, and resurrection, applied by the Holy Spirit; the saint is baptized in the name (singular) of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; the very Christian identity is constituted by the Trinity.

The heretical anti-Trinitarian movements are the historic corruption that the orthodox church has confronted across every generation. Arianism in the fourth century denied the Son’s full deity, making Him a created firstborn; Nicaea confessed instead theos ek theou, phōs ek phōtos, theos alēthinos ek theou alēthinou, gennetheis ou poiētheis, homoousios tōi patri—God of God, Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father. Modalism (in its various ancient and modern forms) denies the distinct persons, treating Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as modes or manifestations of one person; the orthodox tradition has consistently confessed the three distinct persons in one essence. Modern movements—Jehovah’s Witnesses denying Christ’s deity, Unitarianism reducing the Trinity to one person, certain Word-of-Faith and Oneness Pentecostal movements distorting the Trinity in various ways—are the contemporary recurrences of the same ancient errors. The recovery is the precise New Testament application of theos: to the Father (uniformly), to the Son (explicitly in John 1:1; 20:28; Heb 1:8; Titus 2:13; 2 Pet 1:1; 1 John 5:20), and (by inference) to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3-4)—one God in three persons, eternally distinguished, eternally united, the Trinity Christians worship and the only true God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek theos (God): the chief NT noun for the deity, LXX translation of the Hebrew Elohim; applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit; the foundation of Trinitarian doctrine and the structural noun of Christian theology.

expand to see more

Greek theos (G2316) — God (over 1300 NT uses).

Hebrew Elohim (H430) — God (the most common Hebrew word for God; the plural form with singular verb agreement signaling the divine plurality-in-unity later articulated in Trinitarian doctrine).

Hebrew El (H410) — God (the cousin term).

Greek theotēs (G2320) — Godhead, deity (Col 2:9, “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”).

Usage

"And the Word was God—John 1:1 anchors the deity of Christ in the precise application of theos to the Word."

"My Lord and my God—Thomas’s confession after the resurrection is the disciple’s explicit recognition of Christ’s deity."

"Generic-deism flattens theos into a religiously-neutral category; anti-Trinitarian heresies refuse its precise NT applications; biblical theos is the One God in three persons whom Christians worship."
